b99fa541-88b0-4947-80a2-b86b7cf59e89: The optimum is marked at the highest point of the curve, at about 40 °C. The falling part of the curve above 40 °C (from about 40 °C to 60 °C) is labelled "enzyme denatured".
fc3da5ee-4939-47c9-9b62-f523e48e2841: Between 40 °C and 60 °C the rate falls steeply, to almost zero at 60 °C. The high temperature breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the enzyme in shape, so the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured. The substrate no longer fits the active site, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
a33b49b1-7daf-4d8b-b2f7-ab82920b1d9a: Measure how much product is formed (or substrate used up) at timed intervals, for example the volume of oxygen collected in a gas syringe every 30 s, or the colour change measured with a colorimeter. The rate is the amount formed ÷ time, or the gradient of the first part of the graph.
1898b8d7-8211-4a26-a90d-b40f606c9ba0: Anabolic reactions build larger molecules from smaller ones (often by condensation) and use energy, for example protein synthesis or photosynthesis. Catabolic reactions break large molecules into smaller ones (often by hydrolysis) and release energy, for example digestion of starch or cell respiration.
490e5d99-bce1-4ad4-a3da-ef33c410c63c: Graph: substrate concentration on the x-axis and rate of reaction on the y-axis; the curve rises steeply from the origin, then bends and levels off (plateau). At low substrate concentration, adding substrate means more collisions with free active sites, so the rate rises. At high concentration all the active sites are occupied (the enzyme is saturated), so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor and the rate stays constant.
71c88472-c029-46e7-9bfa-3c646292d520: Enzyme and substrate molecules move randomly in solution. A reaction can only happen when the substrate collides with the active site in the correct orientation; it then binds, forming an enzyme–substrate complex, and the products are released. Higher kinetic energy (higher temperature) gives more frequent successful collisions, so the rate increases. Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Away from the optimum, the pH changes the charges on the amino acids and breaks ionic and hydrogen bonds in the active site, so its shape changes. The substrate binds less well or not at all, so activity falls; at extreme pH the enzyme is denatured.
1790f3fe-b999-4e67-a600-325e6de409f8: X is a competitive inhibitor: at high substrate concentration the rate with X rises to the same maximum as curve A. Y is a non-competitive inhibitor: its maximum rate is lower (about half) and does not reach the maximum of A however much substrate is added.
bd232d66-48f4-4322-8ba4-82fe4116ef7b: Inhibitor X is similar in shape to the substrate and competes with it for the active site. When there is much more substrate, a substrate molecule is more likely than X to occupy each active site, so the effect of X becomes smaller.
5f6e2c51-26f9-428e-be19-bd3bf34a9802: Y binds to the enzyme at a site other than the active site (an allosteric site). This changes the shape of the active site, so the substrate can no longer bind and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
868c9d01-d368-4058-bc77-0a928224eb67: Diagram: y-axis energy, x-axis progress of reaction. Reactants start at a higher level and products end at a lower level (exergonic). Two curves: a tall peak without the enzyme and a lower peak with the enzyme; the activation energy is labelled for each as the height from the reactants to the peak. Label: the enzyme binds the substrate, stressing its bonds and holding it in the right orientation, so less energy is needed and more molecules have enough energy to react, so the reaction is faster.
8f93bf8b-2e87-4da3-9f16-249a7d86accf: When isoleucine (the end product) builds up, it binds to the allosteric site of the first enzyme in the pathway, threonine deaminase. This changes the shape of the active site so threonine cannot bind, and the pathway slows or stops. When isoleucine levels fall it detaches and the pathway restarts, so negative feedback keeps the level steady; the inhibition is reversible and non-competitive.
32074b65-c722-4589-b6a2-f44b845cb50b: Both are series of steps, each catalysed by its own enzyme. In a linear pathway the starting substrate is converted through intermediates to an end product, for example glycolysis (glucose to pyruvate). In a cyclical pathway the starting compound is regenerated at the end, so intermediates are recycled, for example the Krebs cycle or the Calvin cycle.
8053434a-f03e-41df-add1-0b7e7d1fe670: Penicillin inhibits the bacterial enzyme transpeptidase, which forms cross-links between peptidoglycan chains in the cell wall. Penicillin binds irreversibly (covalently) to the active site, a mechanism-based inhibition, so no new cross-links are made. The cell wall is weakened, and as the bacterium grows, water enters by osmosis and the cell bursts. Resistance arises by random mutation: the active site of transpeptidase changes so penicillin no longer binds, or the bacteria make penicillinase (beta-lactamase), which breaks penicillin down. Resistant bacteria survive treatment and reproduce, so by natural selection the resistance allele becomes more common, especially when antibiotics are overused.
0ce5d21a-9869-4095-a783-b1184c33318e: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme in the pathway that makes cholesterol in the liver. Statins are similar in shape to the substrate and compete for the active site, so less cholesterol is made and blood (LDL) cholesterol falls, lowering the risk of coronary heart disease. However, they can cause side effects such as muscle pain, must usually be taken long term, and work best alongside a healthy diet and exercise.
17f8b9b5-5003-4a5c-a597-685808bfeab1: Cell wall: a label line touching the boundary between two neighbouring cells. Nucleus: a label line touching the round, darker structure inside one cell.

47a0405f-24bd-456d-b057-81bb4b8c3bc2: Embryonic stem cells can become any type of cell, so they could treat more conditions, such as replacing dopamine-producing neurones in Parkinson's disease or nerve cells after spinal cord injury. However, obtaining them destroys an embryo, and some people believe an embryo has a right to life, so their use is ethically controversial and restricted by law in some countries. Adult stem cells, such as those in bone marrow, avoid destroying embryos, and using the patient's own cells avoids rejection; bone marrow transplants already treat leukaemia successfully. But adult stem cells can only become a few cell types and are harder to find and grow. Socially, these treatments give hope to patients and families, but religious and cultural views differ. Economically, treatments are expensive to develop and may only be available to people who can pay. Overall, adult stem cells are more acceptable and already in use, while embryonic stem cells offer more potential but raise greater ethical concerns.
22d2afc1-2938-416d-aec8-382ba9def69f: Benefit 1: it could reduce the shortage of donor organs and shorten waiting lists. Benefit 2: organs printed from the patient's own cells would not be rejected, so immunosuppressant drugs would not be needed. Limitation: it is very expensive and still experimental; complex organs with blood vessels are hard to print and long-term safety is unknown.
f2de3567-fed1-4f31-a018-e74fb4997594: Privacy: profiles may be kept without consent (including those of innocent people) and could be misused, shared or used to reveal family relationships or health information.
